name: Lee's Place (Hardscrabble): the farm cabin on the South Branch
aka: Messrs. Russell and Lee's cabin (Captain Heald, 15 April 1812)
Lee's place, later known as Hardscrabble (Moses and Kirkland)

documented_range.note: THE OPENING IS A DATED MENTION AND THE CLOSE IS A BOUND THIS PROJECT CHOSE. It opens on 6 April 1812, the evening Captain Heald's letter of 15 April puts a party at 'Messrs. Russell and Lee's cabin, in a field on the Portage branch of the Chicago river' (Moses and Kirkland 1895, p. 43, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 6878-6885): the first dated day a source puts the cabin on the ground. It is older than that, and no source says how much: Currey has it 'built some time after Fort Dearborn had been established' (the plate's caption, Gutenberg #52346 plain text lines 1482-1487), so after 1803. It closes at the end of 1822, the last year a source puts a house on the same premises: Gurdon Hubbard, as Hurlbut printed him (data/research/books/text/hurlbut_chicago_antiquities_28_36.txt lines 58-61), sets John Crafts's trading house 'about half a mile below Bridgeport, ("Hardscrabble" - the same premises, where in April 1812, two murders were committed by the Indians)', and 'In 1822, Crafts succumbed, and engaged himself to the American Fur Company' (same, lines 61-64). Whether Crafts traded from Lee's cabin or built his own is not known, so the close is a bound and not a reading (L-1812-lees-place-2509). It is out of 1835 either way.

position.symbolic_location: Lee's Place, on the north-west bank of the South Branch half a mile below the later canal mouth at Bridgeport (T-2501's ruled reach), about 30 m back from the bank at the reach's station; local E -1661.1..-1645.7, N -4229.2..-4217.4, its river front facing south-south-east across the channel.
position.note: SEATED ON T-2501's RULING, NOT MEASURED. data/terrain/1812_hardscrabble_site.json rules the farm onto a REACH of the north-west bank, 0.25 to 0.75 mi below Bridgeport by river, with its station half a mile below (Hubbard's 'about half a mile below Bridgeport ... on the north side of the river, (south branch)'), at local E -1638.9, N -4249.5; it says the cabin's place on that reach is this ticket's. THE RULING HERE: the cabin's centre stands 30 m inland of the station along the bank's own normal (bearing 331 degrees), on T-2502's apron at its 1.31 m land grade, with its long front facing the river (rotation 151 degrees, the normal reversed). Why near the bank: every account puts the cabin by the water - Wau-Bun has the men's canoes 'tied near the bank' in sight of the cabin door, Currey says the farm and the fort talked 'by means of canoes', and the 1912 plate (currey_1912_hardscrabble_plate, tier 5) draws the house a few rods back from the bank inside the field's fence with a canoe below it. The 30 m is this project's (L-1812-lees-place-2509); the plate gives no distance. Why the station's normal and not a point up or down the reach: no source distinguishes one place on the reach from another, so the cabin takes the one point the ruling names. The bearing to the fort is about 3.3 miles in a straight line, inside Heald's 'about three miles from the garrison' (T-2501's own test). If the reach moves, the cabin moves with it.

derivation.reason: Not by any of validate.py's methods (platted corner, traced waterline, street frontage): the cabin is seated on T-2501's ruled reach of the 1812 South Branch, which the structure-position derivations do not read. The seat is a stated ruling recorded as L-1812-lees-place-2509.

footprint.note: Unattested in size. Proportioned on the 1912 plate, which draws a long, low house whose river front is about two and a half times its gable end and carries three doors and six windows: 48 x 18 ft (14.6 x 5.5 m). The plate is a retrospective picture (tier 5) and gives no measure, so the size is this project's (L-1812-lees-place-2509). A log house this long is two pens under one roof, which the plate's three doors also suggest; the archetype builds it as one.

stories.note: One storey. Heald and Currey both call it a cabin, and the 1912 plate draws a single low storey with nothing in the roof.

wall_height_m.note: Unattested. About eight feet of log to the plate; the plate's front is low, a little over a door's height to the eave.

construction.note: Currey 1912: 'On this tract stood a log cabin in which a number of men employed by Lee lived and carried on the work of the farm' (Gutenberg #52346 plain text lines 1456-1457), and 'the log house at Hardscrabble' (lines 1495-1496).

roof_type.note: The 1912 plate draws a dark gable roof whose ridge runs along the river front. A retrospective picture, so inferred and not attested.

roof_pitch_deg.note: Unattested. Read off the plate's ridge: T-2509's 30 degrees put the ridge's right end at y 163.2 px through the camera against the drawing's 167.1, and 24 degrees brings it down to the drawing, which also leaves the stack's head standing just clear of the ridge as the plate draws it (T-2511). The plate is tier 5.

chimneys.note: One stack, which the 1912 plate draws standing outside one gable end: the LEFT, upstream gable as seen from the river, at its front corner (chimney_end, chimney_cross_m).

front_set_out.note: The river front's nine openings in the order the 1912 plate draws them from the downstream end: window, door, window, window, door, window, window, door, window — three doors and six windows. Each centre is the plate's opening read on a 1 px grid (a darkness profile across the front at y 191-196 px for the windows and 198-203 px for the doors) and carried onto the front wall through the plate's solved camera (data/reference_views/lees_place_cabin_1812/currey_1912_hardscrabble.json); one plate pixel is about 0.2 m of wall, so each centre is good to about that. A retrospective picture (tier 5), so inferred and not attested; the three doors are also what a two-pen house under one roof would show (the footprint's note).

door_w_m.note: Unattested. The plate's three doors read 1.17, 1.30 and 1.34 m wide through its camera, each edge good to about 0.2 m; 1.2 m is taken from that reading (L-1812-lees-place-2511).

door_h_m.note: Unattested, and NOT the plate's reading. Its door heads read 1.49-1.54 m over grade through the camera, which is lower than a man walks under; the build keeps a low cabin door of 1.7 m and the plate's line of heads, so the heads stand about 1 px higher in the render than in the drawing (L-1812-lees-place-2511).

window_w_m.note: Unattested. The plate's six windows read 0.80-1.07 m wide through its camera (mean 0.89), each edge good to about 0.2 m (L-1812-lees-place-2511).

window_h_m.note: Unattested. The plate's windows read 0.78-0.82 m tall through its camera, their heads level with the doors' (L-1812-lees-place-2511).

front_shutters.note: The 1912 plate draws the six windows as plain dark lights with nothing beside them.

chimney_end.note: The 1912 plate stands the stack outside the LEFT gable as seen from the river, which is the upstream end, the footprint's +x end.

chimney_cross_m.note: Slid to the front corner of the upstream gable (the builder holds it inside the corner, here 2.27 m from the gable's middle). Through the plate's camera a centred stack would stand at x 289-302 px against the drawing's 310-325; at the front corner it stands at 308-322, and its head at y 165 px against the drawing's 165. A stack at the front of the gable also leaves the gable's back half for the lean-to the plate draws beyond it.

lean_to.note: The 1912 plate draws a lower gabled shed beyond the stack at the upstream end, its gable to the river and its face drawn in vertical strokes, as boards are. Built as a plank lean-to against the gable, tucked in behind the stack. The plate's own perspective for it disagrees with the main roof's, so its size is read only roughly.

lean_to_length_m.note: Unattested. Sized so its far corner lands at the plate's x 297.5 px through the camera (L-1812-lees-place-2511).

lean_to_width_m.note: Unattested. Back from the stack's back face across the gable. The plate draws the lean-to flat to the viewer, against the main roof's perspective, so through the camera any depth it has shows as an upstream side the drawing does not draw; 1.8 m keeps that side to about 17 px while leaving a room a shed could be (L-1812-lees-place-2511).

lean_to_wall_m.note: Unattested. Its eave reads at y 184 px on the plate; 2.2 m puts it at 183.8 through the camera (L-1812-lees-place-2511).

lean_to_pitch_deg.note: Unattested. The plate draws the lean-to's gable steeper than the house's, its apex at y 172 px; 45 degrees puts it there through the camera, about (L-1812-lees-place-2511).

log_finish.note: THE RULING T-2509 LEFT OPEN: whitewash or the wash drawing's shorthand. Built whitewashed, at the reconstructed tier. The plate draws the walls of the house smooth and pale with no courses and no notched corners, while it draws the lean-to's boards in strokes, the fence's rails one by one and the stack's shaded side dark: its maker drew texture where he saw it, so the pale wall is more likely a coat than a convention. Lime whitewash on a log house is the common frontier finish. No source here says the cabin was whitewashed, and a monochrome wash drawing a century later cannot prove it (L-1812-lees-place-2511).

roof_condition.note: Tone, not colour: the 1912 plate draws the roof much darker than the walls, nearly black, which a weather-blackened shake or shingle roof reads as in a monochrome print. Darkened is the sheet's weather-blackened condition (generators/common/materials.py, ROOF_CONDITIONS). What the roof was covered with is not said.

chimney_head_m.note: Unattested. The plate's stack tops out at y 164-165 px, a little over the ridge; 4.2 m over grade puts its head at y 161.5 through the camera, 0.46 m over the 24 degree ridge, which is the eighteen inches the town's by-law of 1835 asks of every stack and which tools/measure_stack_ordinance.py holds every building to. The drawing's own head (about 3.9 m) would stand 0.16 m over the ridge. The archetype's rule (0.72 m over the ridge, 4.46 m here) is not used because the stack stands at the eave corner, not by the ridge (L-1812-lees-place-2511).

phases.change_note: Built T-2509 (2026-10-15), piece 1 of T-2503: the farm cabin at Lee's Place in the 1812 scene, on T-2501's ruled reach and T-2502's apron ground. Rebuilt T-2511 (2026-10-15) to the plate: the river front's three doors and six windows, the stack at the upstream gable's front corner, the plank lean-to behind it, whitewashed logs and a darkened roof.

function.note: The farm's cabin, where Lee's hired men lived and worked the farm; Lee and his family lived in their house near the fort (lee_house_1812). Currey 1912 (lines 1456-1458); Heald calls it 'Messrs. Russell and Lee's cabin, in a field'.

research_note: LEE'S PLACE, LATER HARDSCRABBLE: the farm Charles Lee worked on the South Branch, and its log cabin, where on 6 April 1812 Liberty White and a Canadian Frenchman whose name Heald did not know (Debou in Currey) were killed by a war party Heald took to be Winnebagoes; the discharged soldier and Lee's son escaped across the river and ran to the fort. WHERE: four placings that do not all meet (data/terrain/1812_hardscrabble_site.json, T-2501): Heald's three miles from the garrison and Moses and Kirkland's north-west bank near the forks agree with the ruled reach; Currey puts it at the canal's mouth itself, half a mile above, and his caption's four miles from the river's mouth falls a mile short of both. The scene card `where_lees_place_stood` says so to the visitor. WHAT IT LOOKED LIKE: only the 1912 plate (currey_1912_hardscrabble_plate), drawn a century later by a maker the book does not name; it is tier 5, and the cabin is built toward it through the image gate (data/reference_views/lees_place_cabin_1812/). WHAT IS NOT BUILT: the haystacks Wau-Bun puts with the cattle on the OPPOSITE bank (T-2510), the plate's three outbuildings, and the cattle. It carries review_required because its card and this record speak of a killing in the war of 1812, an event of Winnebago and Potawatomi history as much as the settlers', and the 1812 scene waits on the review T-0472 holds it for. Nobody is drawn in or near it (L1).
